header: Present: Mr. Muhammad Saleem Awan, Advocate for
Mr. Zulfiqar Ali Tanoli, Advocate for respondents.
body: SYED MUDASSER AMEER, J. – Through these connected revision petitions, the petitioners have called in question two judgments and decrees dated 25.02.2013 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-IV, Mansehra, in Civil Appeals Nos.49/13 and 61/13 of 2011. Both appeals arose out of two cross-suits concerning Khasra No.7372, measuring 17 kanals and 13 marlas, situated at Mouza Baffa Lughmani Lehari Teetwal, District Mansehra. The learned trial Court had decided both suits through a common judgment and decree dated 31.01.2011. Since the controversy, the property and the material evidence are substantially common, both revisions are being decided through this consolidated judgment.

2. The dispute concerns the transfer of occupancy-tenancy rights by Fazal-e-Haq to Wasil Khan through Mutation No.311 dated 14.06.1948 and the subsequent conversion of those rights into ownership through Mutation No.1401 dated 19.12.1952, after deposit of compensation. The petitioners claim through Wasil Khan. Their case is that the entire Khasra was transferred to their predecessor, who was delivered possession and subsequently acquired proprietary rights upon payment of compensation. The entries subsequently appearing in the revenue record in favour of other persons were, therefore, liable to be corrected.

3. Suit No.83/1 was instituted by the petitioners on 02.06.2004. The learned trial Court decreed the suit, holding that Wasil Khan had purchased the occupancy rights of Fazal-e-Haq through Mutation No.311 and subsequently acquired ownership through Mutation No.1401. The respondents, namely, the legal heirs of Abdullah Jan, preferred Civil Appeal No.49/13. The learned Additional District Judge partly accepted the appeal, maintaining the petitioners' claim only to the extent of Fazal-e-Haq's share and dismissing their claim in respect of the remaining property.

4. The other suit, No.96/1, was instituted on 23.05.2007 by the legal heirs of Abdullah Jan, claiming a one-third share in the same property. Their case was that Abdullah Jan had also been an occupancy tenant and had neither transferred his rights nor delivered possession to Wasil Khan. It was alleged that Wasil Khan had purchased only the occupancy rights of Fazal-e-Haq but fraudulently deposited compensation for the entire property and procured Mutation No.1401. The learned trial Court dismissed the suit. However, the learned Additional District Judge, through judgment in Civil Appeal No.61/13, accepted the appeal and decreed the suit.

5. Learned counsel for the parties have been heard at length and the entire available record has been examined. The principal controversy is not whether Abdullah Jan's name appeared in some of the historical revenue entries as an occupancy tenant. That fact is borne out by the record. The real questions are: what interest was transferred by Fazal-e-Haq to Wasil Khan; whether the transfer related to the entire Khasra and possession thereof; what legal effect followed from Mutation No.1401; and whether the legal heirs of Abdullah Jan established any independent proprietary right in the property which could justify the declaration granted by the appellate Court.

6. The revenue record for the years 1930-31, 1940-41 and 1946-47 does mention Fazal-e-Haq and Abdullah Jan, amongst others, as occupancy tenants. This circumstance cannot be ignored. But it does not, by itself, establish that Abdullah Jan possessed a separately demarcated portion of Khasra No.7372 or that the entire land was in his exclusive possession. More importantly, the evidence must be examined as a whole, including the subsequent transactions and the actual state of possession.

7. Mutation No.311 dated 14.06.1948 identifies Khasra No.7372, measuring 17 kanals and 13 marlas. It records the transfer of occupancy-tenancy rights by Fazal-e-Haq in favour of Wasil Khan. The transaction was not confined to an unidentified or unspecified portion. It related to the entire identified holding. The trial Court also examined the Fards and the relevant revenue record and found that Fazal-e-Haq had been in possession of the property and that possession passed to Wasil Khan following the transaction.

8. The oral evidence materially supports that conclusion. The admissions made by the defence witnesses during cross-examination were not properly appreciated by the learned appellate Court. Those admissions establish that Fazal-e-Haq had transferred the entire suit property to Wasil Khan and that the possession of the property remained with Fazal-e-Haq and thereafter with Wasil Khan's successors. The evidence also supports the existence of an arrangement or private adjustment between Fazal-e-Haq and the other interested persons. The learned trial Court specifically noticed the private partition between Fazal-e-Haq and the predecessor of defendants No.1 to 3. The appellate Court rejected the trial Court's conclusion without properly examining the admissions and the circumstances in which the transaction had taken place.

9. There is another important feature. Almost all the defence witnesses admitted that Abdullah Jan had spent his life outside the village, initially in Bengal and subsequently in Karachi or elsewhere. He was not residing in the village or cultivating the disputed property. The witnesses also acknowledged the joint character of the original holding. These admissions must be read with the uninterrupted possession of Fazal-e-Haq and, subsequently, Wasil Khan and the transfer of possessory rights of the entire holding as recorded in Mutation No.311.

10. The fact that the land formed part of joint ownership does not render the transaction ineffective. The law recognizes the right of a co-sharer, who is in exclusive possession of a specific portion of joint property, to transfer his possessory rights in that property. The transferee steps into the shoes of the transferor and is entitled to retain possession until an actual partition takes place. The rights of the other co-sharers can be adjusted at the time of partition.

11. In Feroz v. Sher and others (PLD 1985 SC 254), the honourable Supreme Court held that although a co-sharer cannot transfer full proprietary rights beyond his own entitlement, the transfer of possessory rights in specific land is valid to the extent of the rights held by the transferor. The vendee is entitled to retain possession until partition, subject to adjustment of the respective rights of the co-sharers.

12. The same principle was reiterated in Amir Shah v. Ziarat Gul (1998 SCMR 593). The Court recognized that a vendee of a cosharer in exclusive possession acquires the same rights as the vendor, neither more nor less, and may retain possession of the specific property until partition, provided that the area transferred does not exceed the vendor's entitlement. This principle was followed by this Court in Wahid Zaman and others v. Misal Khan and others (2013 YLR 2732).

13. These authorities are directly relevant. The entire Khasra was identified in the transaction. Fazal-e-Haq was in possession of the entire property. Possession was delivered to Wasil Khan. The fact that the property formed part of a larger joint holding did not invalidate the transfer or require the vendee to surrender possession merely because the precise shares had not been adjusted. Any genuine claim of another co-sharer could be worked out through partition, where the respective entitlements could be determined. No such adjustment had taken place before the institution of these proceedings. Nor did the respondents establish any separate and demarcated portion of the Khasra which had remained in their predecessor's possession.

14. The learned appellate Court, therefore, fell into error by treating the presence of Abdullah Jan's name in the historical revenue record as sufficient to defeat the transaction made by Fazal-e-Haq. It failed to distinguish between the transfer of proprietary title and the transfer of an occupancy or possessory interest in a specific holding.

15. The matter does not end with Mutation No.311. The subsequent Mutation No.1401 dated 19.12.1952 is equally, if not more, significant. It records the conversion of the occupancy-tenancy rights into ownership in favour of Wasil Khan after deposit of compensation under the relevant notification, through Treasury Challan No.3766. This is not merely a subsequent entry of possession. It records a statutory conversion of tenancy rights into proprietary rights.

16. At the relevant time, the matter was governed by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Tenancy Act, 1950, as it then stood. Section 4 of the Act provided different modes for acquisition of ownership by occupancy tenants. An occupancy tenant who paid no rent beyond land revenue, rates and cesses acquired ownership without compensation. A tenant paying cash rent, or rent partly in cash and partly in kind, could acquire full ownership upon payment of the prescribed compensation. Section 4-A, inserted in 1952, separately dealt with tenancies where rent was paid by division of produce and provided for acquisition of ownership in proportion to the tenant's share of the produce retained by him.

17. Thus, the statutory scheme distinguished between an occupancy right and the proprietary title subsequently acquired by satisfying the prescribed conditions. In Haji Muhammad Yaqoob v. Fazalur Rehman and another (PLD 1986 Peshawar 147), this Court held that an occupancy tenant does not become a co-sharer in the proprietary holding merely by virtue of his occupancy status. Acquisition of proprietary rights depends upon fulfilment of the conditions prescribed under Sections 4 and 4-A of the Act.

18. In the present case, Mutation No.1401 expressly records the conversion of tenancy into ownership after payment of compensation. The Treasury Challan is also referred to in the revenue record. The transaction was reflected in the subsequent revenue entries. The respondents have not established that the compensation was fictitious, that the mutation was forged, or that the statutory conversion had been procured through fraud. Their allegation that compensation was deposited fraudulently for the entire property remained unsubstantiated.

19. The fact that the record may have shown other persons as occupancy tenants in earlier years does not, without more, invalidate the statutory conversion recorded in favour of Wasil Khan. The respondents were required to establish the independent nature and extent of their predecessor's rights, the mode of rent applicable to his tenancy, and the statutory basis upon which those rights had matured into ownership. They failed to do so.

20. The legal effect of the decision of the Shariat Appellate Bench also requires consideration. In Sultan Khan v. Government of N.W.F.P. (1989 SCMR 2012), the honourable Supreme Court declared Section 4 of the NWFP Tenancy Act, 1950, and the relevant Rules repugnant to the Injunctions of Islam, but directed that the decision would take effect from 23.03.1990. The statutory provisions and their self-executory consequences remained protected until that date. The subsequent decision in Sardar Muhammad Yousaf v. Government of Pakistan (PLD 1991 SC 760) also recognized the transitional position.

21. The consequence is that an occupancy tenant who had already acquired proprietary rights by fulfilling the statutory conditions before 23.03.1990 retained those rights. On the other hand, a person who had not acquired proprietary ownership by that date could not claim such ownership thereafter merely on the basis of an old occupancy entry.

22. In Gul Rehman and others v. Muhammad and others (2010 CLC 318), this Court explained that a person whose occupancy rights had not matured into ownership under the statutory scheme by 23.03.1990 could not thereafter claim proprietary rights under the provisions which had ceased to operate. The status of such a person could, at the highest, be that of a tenant-at-will. The same principle was considered in Noor Maidar v. Altaf Ahmad Khan (2014 YLR 468).

23. Applying these principles, the legal position of the two branches becomes clear. Wasil Khan acquired the occupancytenancy rights from Fazal-e-Haq in 1948. The property was thereafter converted into ownership through Mutation No.1401 in 1952 upon payment of compensation. The conversion thus took place long before the cut-off date of 23.03.1990.

24. The legal heirs of Abdullah Jan, on the other hand, have not established that their predecessor acquired proprietary rights under Section 4 or Section 4-A of the Act. They have not proved that he occupied a separately identifiable portion of the property, that he fell within the category of tenants entitled to acquire ownership without compensation, that he paid the prescribed compensation, or that he acquired a proportionate proprietary share under Section 4-A. Nor have they established how the one-third share claimed in their plaint was calculated.

25. An old entry as an occupancy tenant cannot, by itself, establish ownership. The burden of proving acquisition of proprietary title under the statutory scheme rested upon the plaintiffs in Suit No.96/1. That burden was not discharged. Their claim to a one-third share was thus unsupported by the evidence.

26. The evidence regarding possession further weakens their claim. Their own witnesses, particularly PW-3 Aurang Zeb and PW- 4 Asif Jan, made material admissions during cross-examination. The trial Court noticed that Abdullah Jan had spent his life outside the village and that the suit property had never remained in the possession of the plaintiffs or their predecessor. The Fards and Khasra Girdawari produced by them did not show their predecessor or themselves in the cultivation column as possessors. Instead, Fazale-Haq and thereafter Wasil Khan's successors were reflected in possession.

27. These were not minor discrepancies. They went to the root of the plaintiffs' claim. The learned appellate Court referred to the testimony of Wasil Khan's predecessor's legal representatives regarding the purchase of Fazal-e-Haq's occupancy rights but failed to examine the admissions of the plaintiffs' own witnesses concerning possession. The trial Court had assessed the evidence on this point and recorded a finding against the plaintiffs. The appellate Court displaced that finding without giving adequate reasons or dealing with the material evidence.

28. The conduct of the parties also bears upon the controversy. Mutation No.311 was attested on 14.06.1948. Mutation No.1401 was attested on 19.12.1952. Both transactions remained unchallenged for more than five decades. No one from Abdullah Jan's branch questioned the transfer, the delivery of possession, the deposit of compensation or the conversion into ownership during that long period. The first challenge came through the cross-suit instituted on 23.05.2007, after Wasil's heirs had already instituted their suit for correction of the revenue record in 2004.

29. A person claiming an independent proprietary interest cannot remain silent while another person openly possesses the property under a transaction which is also reflected in the public record, and then seek to reopen the entire matter after decades without explaining the delay or establishing the concealment of the right to sue.

30. The suit of Abdullah Jan's heirs was also barred by limitation. It was a suit for declaration and injunction, governed by Article 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908. The right to sue accrued when the transfer of possession and the subsequent assertion of ownership constituted an actual denial of the proprietary rights now claimed by them. The transactions had been acted upon since 1948 and 1952. The possession of Wasil Khan's branch was open and continuous. The entry of ownership through Mutation No.1401 was also reflected in the revenue record.

31. The plea that the plaintiffs acquired knowledge only after the institution of Suit No.83/1 in 2004 cannot, on these facts, be accepted as sufficient to revive a claim which had remained unchallenged for decades. No particulars of fraud, concealment or misrepresentation were established so as to attract Section 18 of the Limitation Act. Nor was any convincing explanation offered for the failure of Abdullah Jan or those claiming through him to question the transactions during the intervening period.

32. In Mst. Rabia Gula and others v. Muhammad Janan and others (2022 SCMR 1009), the honourable Supreme Court explained that a mere adverse entry in the revenue record ordinarily constitutes an apprehended or threatened denial of rights. Where, however, the beneficiary of the transaction also takes possession of the property, such possession amounts to an actual denial of the rights of the transferor or other claimant. In that situation, limitation runs from the actual denial and cannot be revived merely through succession. The Court also held that an heir cannot obtain a fresh period of limitation where the predecessor, despite knowledge of the transaction and loss of possession, allowed the prescribed period to expire.

33. The same approach is supported by Muhammad Rustam and another v. Mst. Makhan Jan and others (2013 SCMR 299) and Mst. Faheeman Begum (deceased) through LRs v. Islam-ud-Din and others (2023 SCMR 1402). In these cases, the honourable Supreme Court declined to permit successors to reopen long-standing transactions which their predecessors had not challenged during their lifetimes, in the absence of legally sufficient grounds to extend or exclude limitation.

34. The present case is distinguishable from one involving a person who remains in possession as owner but whose name is omitted or wrongly entered in successive revenue records. In Khan Muhammad through LRs v. Mst. Khatoon Bibi and others (2017 SCMR 1476), the Honourable Supreme Court recognized that each fresh wrong entry may furnish a fresh cause of action in a suit for correction of revenue record, provided the aggrieved person remains in actual or constructive possession as owner. That principle supports the petitioners' suit in CR No.118-A, where Wasil's branch remained in possession and sought correction of the revenue record. It does not assist the plaintiffs in Suit No.96/1, whose predecessor's possession had already been displaced and whose proprietary rights were not shown to have matured under the statutory scheme.

35. There is yet another legal impediment in Suit No.96/1. The plaintiffs sought a declaration of one-third ownership and a perpetual injunction, but failed to establish possession. Once the evidence established that the property remained in the possession of Wasil Khan's branch, the plaintiffs could not obtain a mere declaration of ownership while omitting the consequential relief of possession. The proviso to Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, precludes such a declaration where further relief is available but has been omitted. This provides an additional reason why the suit could not have been decreed in the form in which it was instituted.

36. The position in Suit No.83/1, challenged in CR No.118-A, is materially different. Wasil Khan's heirs relied upon two specific and identifiable transactions. Mutation No.311 established the purchase of occupancy-tenancy rights in the entire identified holding from Fazal-e-Haq. Mutation No.1401 recorded subsequent statutory conversion into ownership following payment of compensation. The oral and documentary evidence established continuous possession by the transferor and thereafter by the transferee and his successors. No evidence was produced to establish that the transactions were fictitious or that the possession delivered under them was interrupted by any lawful claim.

37. The petitioners instituted their suit in 2004 after discovering the adverse entries and while remaining in possession. In these circumstances, the principle laid down in Khan Muhammad (2017 SCMR 1476) applies. The suit for correction of the revenue record was not barred merely because the original transactions had taken place decades earlier. The repeated adverse entries could not defeat the petitioners' subsisting rights while their possession continued.

38. The learned appellate Court in Civil Appeal No.49/13 failed to consider the full effect of Mutation No.311, the delivery of possession, the admissions of the defence witnesses and the subsequent statutory conversion through Mutation No.1401. It treated the old occupancy entries in favour of Abdullah Jan as conclusive proof of an independent proprietary share, without determining the statutory basis or extent of that share. It also failed to appreciate the principles governing the transfer of possessory rights in joint property.

39. Similarly, in Civil Appeal No.61/13, the learned appellate Court accepted the suit of Abdullah Jan's heirs without properly examining the trial Court's findings on possession, the admissions of the plaintiffs' own witnesses, the statutory conditions for acquisition of ownership, the limitation issue and the omission of consequential relief. It also failed to determine how the one-third share claimed in the plaint was derived from the historical revenue entries.

40. The jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC is exercised where the subordinate Court has acted illegally or with material irregularity, or has failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in it. The present cases disclose such errors. The learned appellate Court misread and failed to consider material evidence, applied an incorrect legal test to occupancy-tenancy rights and did not give proper reasons on material issues. Its findings, therefore, cannot be sustained.

41. The matter does not require remand. Both suits have already undergone a complete trial. The relevant documents and oral evidence are available on the record. The parties have had full opportunity to establish their respective claims. The controversy can be finally resolved on the existing evidence. A remand after such a long passage of time would serve no useful purpose and would merely prolong litigation which began with transactions dating back to 1948 and 1952.
42. For the foregoing reasons, both revision petitions are allowed in the following terms:

(i) Civil Revision No.118-A of 2013: The judgment and decree dated 25.02.2013 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-IV, Mansehra, in Civil Appeal No.49/13 of 2011 are set aside. The judgment and decree dated 31.01.2011 passed by the learned Civil Judge-XII, Mansehra, in Suit No.83/1 are restored. The suit of the petitioners/plaintiffs for declaration, correction of the revenue record and consequential relief, in terms of the decree of the trial Court, stands decreed.

(ii) Civil Revision No.119-A of 2013: The judgment and decree dated 25.02.2013 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-IV, Mansehra, in Civil Appeal No.61/13 of 2011 are set aside. The judgment and decree dated 31.01.2011 passed by the learned Civil Judge-XII, Mansehra, dismissing Suit No.96/1, are restored.
Consequently, the suit filed by the respondents/plaintiffs, claiming a one-third proprietary share in Khasra No.7372, stands dismissed.

43. The decree in Suit No.83/1 shall operate in accordance with its terms and the legal effect of Mutations Nos.311 and 1401 as discussed above. Any adjustment of an independently established co-sharer's share, if legally available, shall be governed by the law of partition and shall not revive the time-barred claim adjudicated in Suit No.96/1. No proprietary share is declared in favour of the plaintiffs of Suit No.96/1.
44. Both revision petitions are allowed accordingly. There shall be no order as to costs.
Announced.
